concept.name: Triple bottom
concept.definition: A classical bullish reversal pattern in which price in a downtrend tests the same support level three times, forming three roughly equal, well-spaced lows, and completes only when price breaks above the pattern's resistance (the highest of the intervening highs). It is the mirror of the triple top: three successful defenses of the same demand zone. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
concept.intuition: Three times sellers try to force price through the same floor and fail; when the ceiling between those floors finally breaks, the accumulated buying pressure is released.
concept.mechanics: Require a prior downtrend and three comparable lows marking significant turning points, typically over three to six months, with overall volume declining as the pattern develops. Confirmation is a break above the highest intervening high with volume expansion; broken resistance often becomes support on a retest. The target adds the pattern height to the resistance break, though for very long formations the measured target is considered less reliable.
concept.formula: Price target = R + (R - L), where L = average low of the three troughs and R = the resistance level (highest intervening high) at the breakout.
concept.failure_modes: Until resistance breaks, three equal lows also fit a neutral rectangle or a bearish descending triangle, and a downside break of support continues the downtrend instead. Long formations can make the measured price target ineffective.
concept.misconceptions: That holding support three times proves accumulation — the ability to hold support is encouraging, but the pattern is neutral until the resistance breakout confirms it.
concept.example: A stock forms three roughly equal lows near $11 over 13 months, then breaks resistance at $22.50 and closes above it for five consecutive weeks, confirming a major base.
